sections.title: How does the Gravitational force calculator work?
sections.html:
The Gravitational force calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports mass 1 (M) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the Mass 2 (m) (m) (m) (m) (m) (m) (m) (m) (m) (m) (m), the distance (R), the gravitational force (F) and the gravitational constant (G).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Gravitational force calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Mass 1 (M)=(distance (R) ^ 2) × gravitational force (F) ÷ (gravitational constant (G) × Mass 2 (m) (m) (m) (m) (m) (m) (m) (m) (m) (m) (m))
Force mantissa=(gravitational force (F))
Force exponent=(gravitational force (F))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Mass 2 (m) = 10 kg, Distance (R) = 30 m, Gravitational force (F) = 10 N and Gravitational constant (G) = 10. The calculator returns Mass 1 (M) = 9 kg.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Mass 1 (M) = 9 kg should be roughly the size you expected from Mass 2 (m) = 10 kg and Distance (R) = 30 m.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Force, opening in newtons

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Gravitational force calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the Mass 2 (m) (m) (m) (m) (m) (m) (m) (m) (m) (m), the distance and the gravitational force — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

faq.q: What does the Gravitational force calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns mass 1 (M), derived from the mass 2, the distance and the gravitational force. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Gravitational force calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the mass 2, the distance, the gravitational force and the gravitational constant, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter mass 1 (M) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Mass 1 (M) opens in kilograms and the chip beside it offers 29 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Mass 1 (M) = 9 kg. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Gravitational force calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
